📌 Dust Attacks: Why Tiny Amounts Show Up in Your Wallet

Main Points
⏺ A dust attack sends tiny amounts of crypto to many wallets
⏺ The goal is often not immediate theft, but address tracking
⏺ This post explains why “small change” in your wallet can be a surveillance signal

1️⃣ Core Idea — an attacker sends tiny amounts to many addresses and watches where those coins move next.
2️⃣ Why It Matters — this helps link wallets together and potentially de-anonymize users.
3️⃣ Risk Surface — if you mix dust with main funds, analytics can cluster your addresses.
4️⃣ What To Do — don’t move suspicious tiny deposits together with your real funds.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — use wallets that let you hide/freeze dust and separate addresses by purpose.

Final Thoughts

A dust attack looks harmless: someone sent you pocket change. But on-chain, even pocket change can become a tracking tag.

📌 Grayscale launches first Zcash ETF with direct ZEC exposure 

🔖 Grayscale has launched the first exchange-traded fund offering direct exposure to Zcash, bringing the privacy-focused cryptocurrency to NYSE Arca under the ticker ZCSH. Grayscale said Tuesday that the Zcash ETF began trading as a conversion of its existing Grayscale Zcash Trust, giving investors access to ZEC through an exchange-traded product without requiring them to directly hold the cryptocurrency. 

🌐 The fund carries a 2.5% annual sponsor fee. A Grayscale spokesperson said revenue collected from the fee will be directed back into the Zcash ecosystem to support network development, marketing and other initiatives tied to the cryptocurrency. Zcash, launched in 2016, allows users to make shielded transactions that can conceal transaction information through zero-knowledge proofs. The ETF itself holds ZEC while its shares trade through the traditional securities market.

🔗 Grayscale’s launch follows a regulatory process that began with plans to convert its long-running Zcash Trust into an exchange-traded product. Grayscale later submitted several amendments as it moved the registration process forward. Its fifth amended filing, submitted before the weekend ahead of Tuesday’s launch, set the annual sponsor fee at 2.5% and finalized additional terms for the fund.

Kyiv is enduring hours of daytime air raids and air raid warnings as Russia has fired 800 jet-powered drones into Ukraine in four days, using the faster weapons to sustain prolonged waves of attacks

The new-model Shahed drones have a cruising speed of 200mph to 250mph , about double the 115mph achieved by the piston-engine version and beyond the speed of Ukraine’s cheap interceptors, making them harder to stop.

Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, said on Sunday that the jet-powered models now accounted for more than half the drones used by Russia to attack and “wear down” the country.

“There were almost 1,500 drones of all types in these four days alone – about 800 of them jet-powered,” 
the president said. Ukraine was currently relying on combat aircraft to shoot them down, he added.

A Geran-4, the latest jet-powered model, struck an ammunition dump at Myla, a village 15 miles west of Kyiv on Thursday. Thirty-eight people were killed as the strike unleashed hours of secondary explosions in one of the deadliest single attacks of the war, destroying warehouses and damaging nearby homes.

Russia has also made heavy use of the drones in waves of daytime attacks in the past five days, leading to hours of air alerts, particularly in Kyiv. Eight air raid alerts sounded in Kyiv by lunchtime on Monday.

Daytime attacks, although far from unknown, were uncommon previously, prompting some businesses to halt operations until the alert had passed, and leaving residents with the decision of whether to remain indoors, seek shelter, or ignore the warnings entirely.

Close drone threats also force emergency services to leave an attack site, potentially worsening the impact of any fire caused by a hit, as happened when a food storage facility was struck in Boryspil, to the east of Kyiv, earlier this month.

Kremlin forces have attacked warehouses around Kyiv in the past month, in retaliation to a Ukrainian campaign targeting the Wildberries and Ozon distribution chains inside Russia. The attacks have led to food shortages in the shops, but a Ukrainian official urged people not to panic.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelensky on defence technology, urged people “do not give in to rumours, misinformation, and panic” and said that companies were rebuilding supply chains in response to the attacks. “We will not die of hunger,” he wrote in a social media posting.

Shahed drones, with a distinctive delta wing, were originally designed in Iran, and the technology transferred to Russia. The jet Shahed, the 238, was first unveiled by Iran in autumn 2023, and appeared in Ukraine shortly after.

It was not until spring that Russia began to manufacture and deploy its latest jet-powered variant – the Geran-4 – in numbers. 

Russia now makes more jet-powered drones than the original piston-engined variants, in two models, the delta winged Geran-4 and the Geran-5, which looks like a missile with wings.

Beskrestnov said that at least 2,500 of the jet drones had been launched into Ukraine during August, up from 1,500 the month before. Production date stamps found on the bodywork suggest they are being fired within days after being made at a factory in Yelabuga, he added.

Ukraine had successfully devised a range of low-cost ground-launched interceptors fast enough to eliminate a piston-engined Shahed, raising interception rates to above 90%. Over the weekend, the president said that level had to be maintained into the autumn.

Engineers are now racing to make faster interceptor drones able to knock out jet-powered Shaheds, though details are scant. 

“Four companies have tried to develop the relevant interceptor drones, we're trying to be successful,” 
Zelensky said.

📌 What is RSI? The overbought/oversold indicator explained 

🔖 The relative strength index is one of the most widely used momentum oscillators in crypto trading, but most traders misread what it actually measures. This guide breaks down the RSI formula, explains how overbought and oversold signals work in practice, and covers the mistakes that turn a useful indicator into a losing strategy. Most traders learn RSI backwards. They start with the idea that 70 means “sell” and 30 means “buy,” treating the indicator like a traffic light for entries and exits. That mental model sounds logical, but it ignores what RSI actually calculates. The relative strength index does not measure whether an asset is expensive or cheap.

🌐 It measures how aggressively price has been moving in one direction compared to the other. Understanding that distinction is the difference between using RSI as a crutch and using it as a genuine analytical tool. RSI quantifies momentum by comparing the average size of recent up moves to the average size of recent down moves over a defined lookback period. The default period is 14, meaning the calculation considers the last 14 candles on whatever timeframe you are viewing.

📊 Average gain is the sum of all positive price changes over the lookback period divided by N. Average loss is the sum of all negative price changes (expressed as positive numbers) divided by N. Periods with no change count as zero for both. What this produces is a bounded oscillator. When gains completely dominate losses, RS becomes very large and RSI approaches 100. When losses dominate, RS approaches zero and RSI drops toward 0. A perfect balance between gains and losses produces an RS of 1 and an RSI of 50.
